parts.title: The Coffee Price Rise Case: Turn Back the Clock on the Price Tag!
parts.part1:
You go to buy your usual coffee, but then you stop. “Hey, when did you become so fancy?” Tariffs are the first thing you think of. You want to say, “So, you’re to blame!” But a good detective stops and thinks first. Let’s turn back the clock and examine this case.

Reports based on government figures say the average U.S. price of ground coffee rose 41%. That was compared with the same month a year earlier. This is about ground coffee, not a cup in a café. Before coffee wakes you up, its price shocks your wallet awake.

But Reuters says most of the rise in store prices came from bean shortages and higher bean prices. Those shortages began before the summer tariffs. Wait a minute. Our case began before the suspect we watched even appeared.
parts.part2:
The investigation leads us to Brazil. A drought was happening there. People had also stopped hoping that the next harvest would be better. “Will there be enough beans?” Before we think about how to brew them, we must ask if there will be any beans to brew at all.

We turn the pages of the record and find this. In February, before summer, New York’s Arabica coffee futures price reached a record high. This was not the price of ground coffee in stores. It was the market price for trading coffee beans. The market alarm had already sounded.

“So, were tariffs not to blame?” No. That would be deciding too soon, too. Reuters also reported that U.S. tariffs put in place during summer raised the price of the beans themselves. They did play a part. But we must put events in the right order.
parts.part3:
Here is the key point. At the time of that report, the tariff-caused rise had not yet passed through the whole supply chain. It had not fully reached the prices shoppers paid. When bean costs rise, the store price tag does not jump up at once and say, “Got it!” Price rises take time to appear.

In other words, a price tag is not live news. It is like a letter that arrives a little late. You may open it today, but it may not be about something that happened today. It may tell you about an earlier drought, a bean shortage, or high market prices. If you look only at the latest headline, you may name the wrong sender.

Next time, take a second look at a store price tag. Ask, “Why is it expensive?” Then add, “When did this happen?” Coffee may taste bitter, but we want our detective work to be clear. Before that first cup, turn the clock back a little.
parts.in_one_line: The average U.S. price of ground coffee rose 41% from a year earlier, mostly because beans were scarce and cost more. Tariffs also raised bean prices, but their full effect had not reached shoppers, so tags may show older events.

parts.title: The Coffee Price Hike Case: Turn Back the Clock on the Price Tag!
parts.part1:
You go to buy your usual coffee, then stop. “Hey, when did you go upscale?” The first thing that comes to mind is tariffs. You want to say, “So you’re the culprit!” But a great detective takes a breath here. Let’s turn back the clock on this case.

In the United States, the average price of ground coffee rose 41% from the same month a year earlier, according to reports based on government figures. This is about ground coffee, not a cup at a café. Before you buy something to wake you up, the price shocks your wallet awake.

But according to Reuters, most of the rise in store prices came from bean shortages that began before the summer tariffs and from higher prices for the beans themselves. Wait a minute. The case had started before the suspect we had our eye on even appeared.
parts.part2:
The investigation takes us to Brazil. A drought was happening there. Hopes that the next harvest would recover had also faded. “Will there be enough beans?” Before thinking about how to brew them, the question was whether there would be beans to brew at all.

Turn the pages of the record, and we find that in February, before summer, the futures price for Arabica coffee in New York reached an all-time high. This was not the price of ground coffee in stores, but the market price for trading coffee beans. The market alarm had already sounded.

“So, are tariffs off the hook?” No, that would be jumping to conclusions too. Reuters also reported that the tariffs the United States imposed in summer pushed up the price of the beans themselves. They did play a part. But we must get the order of events right.
parts.part3:
The key point is that, at the time of that report, the tariff-driven rise had not yet fully made its way through the supply chain to the prices consumers paid. The moment the cost of the beans goes up, the store price tag does not jump up and say, “Got it!” Price rises take time to show up.

In other words, a price tag is not a live news broadcast. It is a letter that arrives a little late. Even if you open it today, it may not be about something that happened today. It may tell you about an earlier drought or bean shortage, or high prices in the market. If you look only at the latest headline, you may get the sender wrong.

Next time you look twice at a price tag in the store, try adding “When did this happen?” to “Why is it expensive?” Coffee may be bitter, but we want our detective work to be clear. Before that first cup, turn back the hands of the clock a little.
parts.in_one_line: The average U.S. price of ground coffee rose 41% year over year, mostly because of earlier bean shortages and higher bean costs. Tariffs also pushed up bean prices, but their effect had not fully reached shoppers, so price tags can reflect earlier events.
